Posture Color Contrast Type Space Components Motion Logos Motifs Icons Voice Accessibility

Design system showcase

Every rule in the system, shown rather than described

This page is a walkthrough of the Liatrio design system for people. Each section shows the real thing rendering, then explains the rule behind it and why the rule exists. Where two sources disagreed, the conflict is named rather than smoothed over.

The page loads the same token stylesheet and the same Space Grotesk font file that the skill ships, so what you are looking at is the system rendering itself rather than a reproduction of it.

Contents

Twelve sections, top to bottom. Foundations first, then components, then the rules that govern output.

01Visual postureDark-first, technical, organic counterpoint 02Color and token rolesWhich color does which job, and the one-accent rule 03Contrast in practiceMeasured pairings, plus two traps worth knowing 04TypographyOne family, scale, weights, tracking, casing 05Space, shape, elevationSpacing scale, radii by role, borders before shadows 06ComponentsButtons, chips, cards, forms, dividers 07MotionEasing and duration, hover through focus 08Logos and marksVariant per background, clear space, hard limits 09Motifs and imageryTextures, dividers, the layering recipe 10IconographyLucide, and what is not an icon 11Voice and copyPerson, casing, punctuation, word choice 12Accessibility and defectsThe checklist, and two shipped violations
01

Visual posture

Dark-first, high-contrast, technical but organic. A cool graphite surface with precise structure, bright green used as signal, and botanical or textured detail as the counterpoint that keeps it from feeling like a terminal.

Platform enablement

Ship faster without trading away control

Lead copy sits at 15 to 20px in the muted foreground, held to a comfortable measure so the eye has somewhere to rest against the texture.

The signature composition: graphite base, hex texture at 6 percent, a node texture pushed to one side, a protection gradient so type stays legible, then content.
Why dark-first. Liatrio sells engineering credibility to technical buyers. The graphite surface reads as tooling rather than brochure, and it gives the greens somewhere to actually signal. On white, the same greens have nothing to push against — that is the root of the contrast problem in section three.
TraitWhat it means in practice
Flat and technicalHairline borders, compact labels, strong grid rhythm, very restrained shadows.
Signal over decorationGreen appears where something is important. It is never a page fill.
Organic counterpointLiatris botanical imagery or the three-pillar Venn keeps the system from reading as pure infrastructure.
Light is a break, not a modeEditorial pages, print, product screenshots, and deck pages may go light. That does not displace the dark default.
02

Color and token roles

The palette is small. The design system's real contribution is role assignment — deciding which color does which job so that a surface never has to guess.

Primary

Four colors carry the brand. Everything else supports them.

Primary Green
#24AE1D
The hero. Key brand moments, focus rings, primary fills.
Bright Green
#89DF00
The signal. Highlights, active borders, links, trace detail.
Grey 800
#111111
Primary text and dark elements on light surfaces.
White
#FFFFFF
Light backgrounds, and the foreground on dark.

Secondary and semantic

Lime, violet, and lagoon are editorial. Red and orange are reserved — they mean something.

Lime
#C6F135
Enablement pillar, square chips, notch cards.
Violet
#C068F9
Strategy pillar. One per surface, at most.
Lagoon
#00C1DB
Information states and secondary data visuals.
Hot Red
#E63946
Errors and alerts only. Never decorative.
Flame Orange
#F77F00
Warnings only.
Dark canvas
#1A1F23
The default page surface.
Dark elevated
#1E2327
Cards, panels, form fields, section contrast.
Border
#2A3036
Hairline structure. Reached for before shadows.

The foreground ramp

Four steps instead of stacking opacity, so text colors stay predictable and measurable.

Primary foreground — headings and high-emphasis text #FFFFFF · 16.6:1

Muted foreground — body copy and lead paragraphs #CCCCCC · 10.3:1

Subtle foreground — captions, metadata, table labels #999999 · 5.8:1

Faint foreground — dividers and disabled states #666666 · 2.9:1, fails as text

Measured against the #1A1F23 canvas. The first three are safe for body copy. The fourth is not — see the note below.
Watch the fourth step. --fg-faint at #666666 measures 2.89:1 on the canvas, which clears neither the 4.5:1 body threshold nor the 3:1 large-text one. It is usable for non-text purposes such as rules and inactive marks, but it should not carry words a reader needs. Reach for --fg-subtle when the content is text.

One accent per surface

Do
Build Platform Delivery

One accent carries the group. The eye reads the set as related, and any second color that does appear immediately means something.

Do not
Build Platform Delivery

Three accents on three peer items. Nothing is emphasised, the semantic colors lose their meaning, and the surface reads as decoration.

The exception is when the colors are the content: Build, Strategy, and Enablement each own an accent, so a Venn or a pillar row is allowed to show all three at once.

03

Contrast in practice

Every ratio on this page was computed from the WCAG relative-luminance formula against the exact token values. The floors are 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text and non-text UI.

Accents on the dark canvas

This is the environment the palette was designed for, and it shows.

Primary Green

on #1A1F23

Large text only

Hot Red is the one accent that does not clear the body threshold on dark. Use it for borders, icons, and short large labels; put the actual error sentence in the normal foreground.

The same greens on light

This is where the system needs care, and where most off-brand output goes wrong.

Primary Green
2.94:1
on #FFFFFF

Fails at any size
Primary Green
2.79:1
on #F8F9FA

Fails at any size
Bright Green
1.66:1
on #FFFFFF

Fails badly
Grey 800
18.88:1
on #FFFFFF

Passes body
Why the greens fail on white. Both greens are mid-to-high luminance. Against a graphite canvas that is a large luminance gap, which is exactly what makes them read as signal. Against white there is almost no gap left. The color is not the problem; the pairing is. On light surfaces, carry the green in a fill, rule, or icon and set the words in Grey 800.
Do — green as a fill, Grey 800 for the words
What we bring
Engineering enablement that sticks

The eyebrow is 18.88:1. The green still leads the eye, but it is doing it with shape instead of with type.

Do not — green as the text itself
What we bring
Engineering enablement that sticks

2.94:1. Legible enough to pass a casual glance, which is exactly why it keeps shipping. It fails for anyone with reduced contrast sensitivity, and it fails on a projector.

Two traps in the tokens

White on Primary Green is 2.94:1

The token file sets --accent to Primary Green and --accent-fg to white. Read the usual way — foreground for when accent is the background — that pairing fails. A Primary Green fill needs dark text, not white.

White label — 2.94:1
Dark label — 5.65:1

The faint foreground step is not a text color

--fg-faint at #666666 is 2.89:1 on the canvas. It reads as a deliberate fourth step in the ramp, which invites using it for de-emphasised copy, but it does not meet either threshold. Keep it for rules, inactive marks, and decoration.

04

Typography

Space Grotesk, and nothing else. Hierarchy comes from size and weight, never from bringing in a second family. Everything below is rendering in the actual variable font file the skill ships.

The scale

Weights and what each one is for

Three hundred

Four hundred

Five hundred

Six hundred

Seven hundred
H1 only

Tracking has three jobs

Tightened headline

headlines above 28px
Default body tracking, left alone

Eyebrow label

Filled CTA label
0.05em
CTA buttons and chips

Casing

Sentence case is the default. Uppercase is a tool for small tracked labels, not a way to add emphasis.

Do
Ship faster without losing control
Case study

Sentence case headline. Uppercase confined to the 11px chip and the 14px button label, both tracked so the letterforms have room.

Do not
Ship Faster Without Losing Control
Case study

Uppercase at 26px with no tracking is hard to read and reads as shouting. Meanwhile the chip and button lose the treatment that made them scannable.

Why the size ceiling. Uppercase removes ascender and descender cues, so word shapes flatten and reading slows. At 14px and below on a short label that cost is negligible and the gain in scannability is real. On a headline it is all cost.

Monospace

Reserved for code, version tags, token names, and technical labels. It is not a stylistic alternative to Space Grotesk.

Set the canvas with --dark-bg and elevate cards to --dark-bg-2. Release v2026.04.14 introduced the current palette.

05

Space, shape, and elevation

A 4px base scale, radii assigned by component role, and a strong preference for borders over shadows on dark surfaces.

Spacing scale

Ten steps on a 4px base. Component padding clusters at 16, 24, and 32. Section padding lives at 64, 96, and 128.

4

Radii by role

Radius is assigned per component type rather than chosen per instance.

4px

Elevation

On dark surfaces a shadow mostly disappears, so structure comes from hairlines first. Shadows are for things that genuinely float.

border only
shadow-sm
shadow-md
shadow-lg
glow-bright
Left to right: the default, then floating UI, then the green glow that marks an active or focused brand moment.

Grid

PropertyValue
Columns12
GuttersAbout 80px desktop, 24px mobile
Max content widthAbout 1280px
Editorial reading widthAbout 720px
06

Components

These are recipes rather than a component library. They demonstrate the treatment and the tokens; the implementation belongs in whatever stack the target project uses.

Buttons come in two languages

This is the single most commonly mistaken rule in the system, so it is worth being precise about.

Blog
Brand CTAs — square. Filled primary at 16 by 32, filled secondary at 12 by 20, outline at 10 by 24, chips at 4 by 10. The filled variants and the chip are uppercase and tracked at 0.05em. The outline button stays sentence case.
Nav and product chrome — 6px. Header buttons, toolbars, and in-app controls. Sentence case, lighter weight, tighter padding.
Why two shapes. Marketing surfaces and product chrome are doing different jobs. A square CTA is a deliberate, slightly severe brand gesture that reads as intentional at hero scale. Product chrome needs to feel like software, and 6px is the shadcn primitive the site is already built on. Mixing them is what looks wrong — a square 6px button in a toolbar reads as unfinished, and a rounded hero CTA reads as generic.
Do

Square, uppercase, tracked, verb-led. 14px keeps it inside the uppercase allowance.

Do not

Capsule shape belongs to pills. Sentence case at 16px loses the CTA treatment, and "Get started" says nothing about what happens next.

Chips and pills

Blog Case study Strategy
Build Strategy Enablement Information Warning Error
Square chips are solid-filled category tags at 11px, weight 700. Pills are translucent with a tinted border at 12 to 13px. Status pills always pair the color with a word.

Cards

Default card

Elevated surface, hairline border, 12px radius, 24px padding.

Active card

Green-tinted border and an inset ring. No drop shadow.

Notch card

A 20px bottom-right clip. One per page, as a signature.

Cards in a grid do not get drop shadows. The border is the structure, and a shadow on a flat dark grid just muddies the edges.

Forms

Click into a field to see the focus treatment: bright green border plus a 3px translucent ring. Errors use the hot red border and always include a human-readable sentence.

Dividers

Gradient divider — violet to lime, 1 to 2px. The muted midpoint is intentional; it keeps the hairline from reading as a rainbow band.

Circuit divider — a section break between two dark surfaces, pulled about 40px into each. Extracted from the live site component.

07

Motion

Precise, never playful. One easing curve does almost all the work, and duration is chosen by how much of the screen is changing. Hover any panel below to play it.

120ms
Micro and hover
200ms
State changes
320ms
Panels and modals
600ms
Page-level reveals

All four use cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1) — a fast start that settles without overshooting.

Do — settle, do not bounce

The standard curve. It arrives with confidence and stops.

Do not — springy overshoot

Overshoot reads as consumer-app playful, which is the opposite of the engineering credibility the brand is built on.

Interaction states

Hover adds a glow and can lift 1px. Press scales to 0.98 and drops the glow, with no color shift. Focus is a 2px bright-green outline at 2px offset — tab through these to see it.
StateTreatment
EnterFade up from 8 to 16px below. Never from the side.
HoverGreen elements gain a glow or outline; dark surfaces lighten about 6 percent.
PressScale to about 0.98, drop the glow, hold the color.
Focus2px bright-green outline at 2px offset. Never the browser default.
The exceptionThe flame logomark may flicker, rotate, morph, or render in 3D as a hero moment.
08

Logos and marks

Ten SVG variants. The choice is driven by background brightness and by whether the placement is wide or square — not by preference.

Horizontal lockups — the primary

logo_Liatrio.svg
Primary on light surfaces.
logo_Liatrio_reverse-preferred.svg
Primary on dark. The default for most Liatrio surfaces.
logo_Liatrio_reverse.svg
All-white alternative when the full-color flame cannot be used.
logo_Liatrio_black.svg
One-color reproduction and print.

Stacked lockups — secondary only

logo_Liatrio_stacked.svg
Square or near-square placements on light.
logo_Liatrio_stacked_reverse-preferred.svg
Square placements on dark.

These two are the only assets that come from the design-system bundle rather than the website, and they are the only variants with no PNG fallback published.

The flame logomark

logomark_Liatrio.svg
Favicon, app icon, deck corner, loader.
logomark_Liatrio_background.svg
The correct mark for green backgrounds, and for even padding on all sides.
Not permitted
The standard mark on green. The flame loses its edge against the fill — use the square variant.

Clear space

Keep clear space on all sides equal to the height of the lowercase L in the wordmark. The dashed line marks the boundary; nothing else enters it.
NeverBecause
Distort or stretchThe flame geometry is fixed. Non-uniform scaling is immediately visible.
RotateThe mark has an upright reading direction.
RecolorTen variants already exist. If none fits the background, the background is wrong.
Add effectsNo shadows, glows, strokes, or bevels on the logo files.
Use stacked as the header lockupStacked is for square placements. Horizontal is the primary.
09

Motifs and imagery

Texture is atmosphere, not pattern. If a viewer can describe the texture, it is turned up too far.

hexagons.svgTileable hex texture. Shown here at full strength so you can see it — in use it belongs at 4 to 8 percent.
floating-nodes.svgNode-and-trace texture for technical sections. Keep it restrained and to one region.
circuit-traces.pngLow-opacity technical texture for panel detail. Never at full opacity behind text.
liatris-digital.pngThe botanical focal point. Large format only — it is not an icon.
venn-diagram.pngBuild, Strategy, Enablement. An infographic device, always labelled.
A note on the texture colors. The two SVG textures use near-brand greens rather than exact palette values — #9BF233, #3DBF52 and #2DB845 in the hex texture, #A6EE38 in the nodes. At 4 to 8 percent opacity that difference is invisible, so the files are shipped as-is. Do not lift those values into type or components.

The layering recipe

Five steps, in order. Skipping the protection gradient is the usual failure.

Layered composition

Text stays readable because of step five

Graphite base, hex texture, trace detail on one side, focal imagery, then a protection gradient beneath the type.

StepLayer
1Solid graphite base — #1A1F23 or #111111.
2Low-opacity hexagon or circuit texture, at large scale.
3Bright-green trace detail on one region, not everywhere.
4Liatris botanical image or the flame mark as the organic focal point.
5Protection gradient wherever text sits over imagery.

Avoid: generic flowers, warm stock photography, full-opacity busy textures, and green marks on green backgrounds.

10

Iconography

Lucide, confirmed rather than assumed. The brand site publishes a curated 120-icon inventory and renders Lucide throughout.

Import icons as components rather than pasting paths:

import { Rocket, ShieldCheck, Workflow } from "lucide-react";

The full 120-name inventory lives in the skill at references/liatrio-brand-site.md. Prefer a name from that list before reaching outside it.
RuleDetail

The flame is the brand iconFavicons, loaders, and deck corners use the logomark, not a Lucide glyph.
The Venn is not an iconIt is an infographic device. It needs labels and room.
Botanical is not an iconLarge format only.
Unicode sparingly→ for an inline CTA is fine. Decorative glyphs are not.
No emojiNot in marketing copy, not in product UI, and never as an icon substitute.
11

Voice and copy

Confident, technical, low-fluff. The register to aim for is a senior engineer who also happens to be good at strategy.

Rewrites

PreferTeach your team to ship the platform themselves

CasingSentence case for headlines, body, navigation, and outline buttons. Title Case only for proper product names.
PunctuationNo exclamation marks in marketing or product UI. Em dashes are welcome. Oxford commas.

12

Accessibility, and two shipped defects

The floors are non-negotiable, and the system is honest about where it currently breaks them.

CheckRequirement

Large text and non-text UIAt least 3:1.

Error · deploy failed

Readable if the color is not perceived at all.

Do not — color alone
deploy-prod-4471

A red dot with no label carries no meaning for a reader who cannot distinguish it from the green one two rows down.

Two surfaces that break the light-surface rule

Recorded here because pretending they do not exist is how they get copied. Both are defects, not precedent.

liatrio.ai/enablement — green eyebrows on white

Two uppercase section eyebrows, "What We Bring" and "How It Works", are set in #24AE1D inside a bg-white section. That is 2.94:1, and at 16 to 18px semibold it does not qualify as large text either, so it misses both thresholds.

The fix is the pattern shown in section three: Grey 800 for the words, with the green carried by a rule beside them.

brand-logo.html — the PREFERRED badge

The preview card renders its badge in #24AE1D on a 14 percent green tint over white, which composites to #E0F4DF for 2.54:1 at 10px.

Built the showcase at `docs/liatrio-design-system-showcase.html` — a single ~23,700px scrolling page with a contents grid at the top and twelve sections, each showing the real thing rendering before explaining the rule and the reasoning behind it. Building it meant actually rendering every rule, and three things fell out that reading the markdown never would have caught.

**The two stacked logo lockups were rendering as solid black.** Both SVGs shipped from the design-system bundle with an empty `<defs>` element, so the `.b`, `.c`, and `.d` classes their paths reference had no fill rules at all. I recovered the intended colors by sampling the bundle's own PNG renders of the same lockups — the pixel counts matched the SVG paths exactly, which also revealed that the two files swap their class letters the same way the horizontal pair does. **The "4–8% opacity" guidance for the textures was wrong.** `hexagons.svg` and `floating-nodes.svg` carry per-element opacity from 0.03 to 0.85 internally, so they're already dimmed. Applying another 6% on top makes them vanish completely — which is exactly what happened on my first render of the masthead. The bundle never specifies that figure anywhere, so it was inferred. I corrected `liatrio-asset-index.md` to say they go in at full opacity and shouldn't drop below about 50%.

Separately, `--fg-faint` at `#666666` is 2.89:1 on the canvas, clearing neither the body nor the large-text threshold despite reading as a legitimate fourth step in the foreground ramp. Both are documented on the page. I also caught the showcase using `--fg-faint` for real text in eight places and raised those to `--fg-subtle`, since a page teaching that rule shouldn't break it.

Every contrast ratio shown was computed from the WCAG relative-luminance formula against the exact token values rather than estimated.
